outcome: No resolution, refutation or proof of the Ω-conjecture has appeared since 26 January 2024; the one in-window event is Goldberg and Hathaway's May 2025 preprint, which proves results conditional on the conjecture and treats it as open, and a search-result claim that Dehornoy's slides report the conjecture proved for a large fragment could not be checked against the slides.
problem_asks: Part 1, the hypothesis: there is a proper class of Woodin cardinals. Part 2, the conclusion: Ω-logic satisfies an analogue of Gödel's completeness theorem. Unpacked, the literature states this as: for every sentence φ of set theory, ZFC ⊢Ω φ if and only if ZFC ⊨Ω φ, that is, every Ω-valid sentence is Ω-provable. The soundness direction (Ω-provable implies Ω-valid) is credited to Woodin in the sources read, so the open content is the converse, that Ω-validity implies Ω-provability. The statement as frozen does not name the class of sentences (the literature restricts to sentences of set theory), nor the two notions it relies on: Ω-validity (truth in forcing extensions, or rank-initial segments of them) and Ω-provability (via universally Baire sets). Both are implicit in the phrase 'Ω-logic'. The problem asks for a completeness theorem for the whole logic, not for any fragment of it.

events.what_happened: Woodin showed in 1985 that, if there is a proper class of measurable Woodin cardinals, generic extensions of V satisfying CH agree on all Σ²₁ statements. Koellner and Woodin (2009) restate this in Ω-logic terms. I did not locate a 1985 write-up; the result is known here only through the 2009 paper's abstract, as quoted on the Cambridge page I opened.
events.delivers: For the Σ²₁ fragment only: under a proper class of measurable Woodin cardinals, ZFC + CH is Ω-complete for Σ²₁ sentences. This is one restricted completeness instance, and it says nothing about sentences of higher complexity.
events.remains: Completeness for all sentences of set theory, which is the content of the Ω-conjecture; and Ω-completeness for theories beyond ZFC + CH at the Σ²₁ level.
events.direction: Consistent with the Ω-conjecture at the Σ²₁ level. It establishes a restricted completeness instance and does not bear on the converse for all sentences.

events.what_happened: Koellner and Woodin, 'Incompatible Ω-Complete Theories', Journal of Symbolic Logic 74(4), December 2009, pp. 1155–1170. The paper shows that ZFC + CH is Ω-complete for Σ²₁ under Woodin's 1985 hypothesis, and that CH is the unique Σ²₁ statement with this property up to Ω-equivalence over ZFC. It also shows that uniqueness fails for stronger candidate theories: if one such theory Ω-implies CH, another Ω-implies ¬CH. A Harvard-hosted copy is dated 25 July 2009; I saw that date only in a search snippet, because the PDF was not readable when I fetched it.
events.revisions: Harvard-hosted copy dated 25 July 2009 (search snippet only). Journal volume dated December 2009. The Cambridge page I opened lists online publication on 12 March 2014. I did not reconcile these dates.
events.delivers: A Σ²₁ instance: ZFC + CH is Ω-complete for Σ²₁ under a proper class of measurable Woodin cardinals, and CH is the unique Σ²₁ statement with that property. Negative result on uniqueness: no single Ω-complete extension of ZFC is forced for larger fragments (the paper names third-order arithmetic and V_λ). It asserts nothing about completeness for all sentences.
events.remains: Completeness of Ω-logic for all sentences of set theory (the Ω-conjecture). The uniqueness question for Ω-complete theories is answered negatively, so it is no longer open.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for mathematical logic; refereed by specialists in set theory and logic
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper after refereeing and published it in volume 74, issue 4

events.direction: Positive for the Σ²₁ completeness instance and negative for uniqueness of Ω-complete theories. It cuts neither way on the full conjecture.

events.what_happened: Woodin, 'The Continuum Hypothesis, the Generic Multiverse of Sets, and the Ω Conjecture', a chapter in a Cambridge volume edited by Kennedy and Kossak (Set Theory, Arithmetic and Foundations of Mathematics). A Cambridge listing gives online publication in October 2011; Meadows (2021) cites it as a 2012 book. The chapter is where the Ω-conjecture is named and argued for, per Wikipedia's Ω-logic article and the secondary sources I read. I did not open the chapter itself.
events.revisions: Cambridge listing gives online publication October 2011. Meadows cites a 2012 book. Not reconciled. Earlier written versions not checked.
events.delivers: Nothing that establishes the conjecture. It states the conjecture and gives heuristic and philosophical arguments for it, including, per the secondary sources, that it is equivalent to the existence of canonical models for large cardinals. No proof is claimed here as far as the secondary sources show.
events.remains: The whole problem: the conjecture itself is stated and argued for, not proved.
events.doubts: Woodin's further inference that a proof of the conjecture would support ¬CH is described as controversial in the Wikipedia Ω-logic article. Dehornoy's encyclopedia article says Woodin's approach rests on a debatable choice of forcing invariance as the starting criterion. Both concern the inference from the conjecture, not the conjecture itself.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture heuristically. Gives no result that moves what the problem asks.

events.what_happened: Toby Meadows (UC Irvine), 'Two Arguments Against the Generic Multiverse', The Review of Symbolic Logic 14(2), pp. 347–379. Published online 2 December 2020; issue dated June 2021; DOI 10.1017/S1755020319000327. The abstract I read says the paper critically examines two arguments against the generic multiverse, both due to Woodin, and that its appendix develops a new inner model for Steel's multiverse theory. A search summary says the first argument centres on a corollary of the Ω-conjecture; I could not confirm that from the full text, which was behind a proxy.
events.revisions: Journal online date 2 December 2020. Preprint date not checked, so the first public written version may be earlier.
events.delivers: Establishes nothing about the Ω-conjecture. It examines arguments against the generic multiverse. If the first argument does use a corollary of the conjecture, that argument is conditional on it, and the paper does not claim to settle the conjecture.

checked_by.who: The Review of Symbolic Logic (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record in philosophical and mathematical logic
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper after refereeing

events.direction: No direction on the conjecture. The paper is an analysis of arguments that use it.

events.what_happened: Woodin's refutation of the Cofinal Branches Hypothesis (CBH) in core model theory. The AIM workshop page 'Recent Advances in Core Model Theory' (undated; the FOM posting I found is from April 2004) says Woodin 'very recently' refuted CBH by a simpler construction, and that the strategic branches hypothesis (SBH), which follows from CBH, is 'crucial to one natural attempt to prove Woodin's Omega-conjecture'. Search summaries also say a refutation under weaker hypotheses dates from 1999 and that the work was never published in full. I did not verify either.
events.revisions: Date of the refutation itself unknown. 2004 is the earliest public written announcement I found.
events.delivers: Refutes CBH, an iteration hypothesis in core model theory. It does not address the Ω-conjecture. At most it removes one proposed route to the conjecture, through SBH, as the workshop describes it.
events.doubts: No written proof located. Known only from workshop announcements and search summaries.
events.direction: Concerns a neighbouring hypothesis, not the Ω-conjecture. It neither proves nor refutes the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Richard Sanchez, 'Strong Omega Consistency', Harvard PhD dissertation in the Department of Philosophy. The title page is dated May 2021; a snippet gives an acceptance date of 5/03/2021. Chapter 3, per the abstract as quoted in a search snippet, uses Ω-logic to define a hierarchy of strongly Ω-consistent large cardinal axioms, and argues that under strong hypotheses they are well-ordered and jointly consistent. The notion of strong Ω-consistency is credited to Woodin. Committee: Koellner, Woodin and Mark Richard. The PDF was not readable when I fetched it, so I have only the snippet.
events.delivers: Concerns a hierarchy of large-cardinal consistency notions expressed in Ω-logic. It does not address the completeness of Ω-logic and does not claim to.

checked_by.qualification: Koellner and Woodin work in Ω-logic, and Woodin introduced it
checked_by.what_they_did: Approved the dissertation, which does not address the conjecture

events.direction: No direction on the conjecture. A different question, discounted for scope.

events.what_happened: Gabriel Goldberg and Dan Hathaway, 'On (Σ²₁)^uB Absoluteness Between V and HOD', arXiv:2505.01393 [math.LO]. v1 submitted 2 May 2025; v2 revised 8 May 2025. The abstract I read, as returned by the fetch tool: assuming a proper class of Woodin cardinals, every (Σ²₁)^uB statement true in V is true in HOD, including with a parameter C ⊆ R whose set and complement have OD universally Baire scales. The proof combines Woodin's Σ²₁ basis theorem for AD+ with Vopěnka's theorem. Upward absoluteness from HOD to V cannot follow from any large cardinal axiom consistent with V = Ultimate L. Section 8 is titled 'The Ω Conjecture'. Corollary 8.3: assuming a proper class of Woodin cardinals, if the Ω conjecture holds in V then it holds in HOD. Proposition 8.6: assuming a proper class of Woodin cardinals, the Ω conjecture holds iff a schema holds: for each large cardinal axiom ∃xφ(x) with V φ-closed, ZFC proves in Ω-logic that V is φ-closed (I read only the first item of the list in full). Corollaries 8.7 and 8.8 assume the Ω conjecture; 8.8 also assumes a proper class of huge cardinals. A search snippet also reports downward absoluteness of Ω-provability from V to HOD; I did not verify that wording in the full text.
events.revisions: v1 2 May 2025; v2 8 May 2025. I read v2 (the HTML version).
events.delivers: Two parts. (1) Not conditional on the Ω-conjecture, given a proper class of Woodin cardinals: (Σ²₁)^uB sentences true in V are true in HOD, including the parameterised version. (2) Conditional on the Ω-conjecture: if it holds in V it holds in HOD (Cor 8.3); under a proper class of Woodin cardinals it is equivalent to Prop 8.6's schema; Cor 8.7 and 8.8 assume it. Neither part establishes the Ω-conjecture for V or for HOD.
events.remains: Completeness of Ω-logic for all sentences in V, the Ω-conjecture, is open. The authors write that 'it is not clear that V satisfies the Ω conjecture' even when HOD does (remark after Cor 8.3). The converse, HOD to V, is unresolved.
events.direction: Neither proves nor refutes the Ω-conjecture. It gives conditional results consistent with it, and the authors treat it as open.

disputes.summary: A search summary of Dehornoy's slides (dehornoy.lmno.cnrs.fr/Talks/Dxg.pdf) says the Ω-conjecture has been proved for a large fragment of the large cardinal hierarchy, with whether that fragment is the whole hierarchy left open. Dehornoy's Universalis article on Ω-logic (site copyright 2026) speaks of the conjecture being established 'un jour' and names no proved fragment. I could not read the slides, which are binary PDFs, so the conflict is unresolved.
Wikipedia dates the introduction of Ω-logic to 1999. A search snippet gives 1990 for the same introduction. I did not verify either date.

summary: No source I read reports a proof, refutation, or counterexample of Woodin's Ω-conjecture, and the conjecture is still called a conjecture everywhere I looked. The Wikipedia Ω-logic article (last revised 1 February 2026 per the fetch) states it as a conjecture. Its only status remark is that the converse is known to hold in all currently known core models. The 'no counterexample is known' phrasing comes from the French encyclopedia article, not Wikipedia. The only in-window (after 26 January 2024) item bearing on it is Goldberg and Hathaway's arXiv:2505.01393 (May 2025). I read its abstract and Section 8 through a fetch tool that returns summaries rather than verbatim text, so my wording of the propositions is partly a paraphrase. Its results are conditional, so they do not move what the problem asks; Dehornoy's encyclopedia article and the Goldberg–Hathaway text both treat the conjecture as open. Earlier events are the Σ²₁ completeness instance (Woodin 1985, restated by Koellner and Woodin, JSL 2009), which is restricted to one fragment, and the Koellner–Woodin uniqueness result, which is negative. Woodin's 2011 chapter states and argues for the conjecture without proof, Meadows (2020) examines arguments that depend on it, Woodin's 2004-era refutation of CBH is about a neighbouring iteration hypothesis, and Sanchez (2021) uses Ω-logic for a different question. Close calls: (a) whether the Goldberg–Hathaway results count as progress, since they transfer the conjecture from V to HOD in conditional form but do not establish it for either; (b) the Dehornoy 'proved for a large fragment' lead, which would be a partial result of unknown date if true, and which the encyclopedia article contradicts. I could not read the slides. (c) Whether Woodin's 2026 AI-related talks ('Can AI Discover Truth Which is Beyond Proof?', IAS, 8 April 2026; 'Truth, proof, and AI', CMSA, 23 September 2026) bear on the problem. The IAS page returned 403 and the CMSA page has no abstract, so I know only the titles. They are talks about AI and truth, and I found no claim that any AI system produced mathematics on the conjecture. AI search: I ran explicit AI-term searches and found no AI-attributed result on the Ω-conjecture or on Ω-logic completeness. The 2026 AI-and-mathematics results I found (OpenAI and AlphaProof-related Erdős problem results, the Epoch FrontierMath Erdős benchmark) are in discrete geometry and combinatorics, not set theory, and nothing I read links them to this problem. ai.none_found is true for every event because no source names a system involved in the conjecture's mathematics. The Goldberg–Hathaway full text, read via the fetch tool, contains no AI, LLM or computer-assistance mention; its funding line is arXiv website boilerplate. Nothing in the record needs to be discounted on AI grounds.
competing_reading: Read the in-window work as partial progress on the Ω-conjecture. Goldberg and Hathaway give an exact equivalence (Prop 8.6) and transfer the conjecture from V to HOD in conditional form. If the Dehornoy 'proved for a large fragment' claim is right, a fragment has been proved, with a date I could not establish. On that reading the problem moved in part, after January 2024, and the record should carry a partial-status event. Against this reading: the Goldberg–Hathaway results are conditional on the conjecture, so they change none of the quantities the problem asks for, and the same authors treat the conjecture as open. The Dehornoy claim comes from a search summary of slides I could not read, and the 2026 encyclopedia article by the same author names no proved fragment.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Readable text of Dehornoy's slides (Talks/Dxg.pdf or Talks/DxgF.pdf), to check the 'proved for a large fragment' claim, its date, and its source. (2) The full text of Goldberg–Hathaway, Prop 8.6 item 2 and Cor 8.8, to confirm the exact dependence on the conjecture and whether any corollary is unconditional on it. (3) A published reply, erratum or citing paper, from 2025 or 2026, that treats the conjecture as settled or still open. (4) Woodin's 2011 chapter, for the exact formulation of the conjecture and any claimed proof sketch. (5) The Woodin talk abstracts or slides for April and September 2026, to confirm they make no claim about AI-produced mathematics.
